items.title: [ScienceDaily] A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study
items.content_html: Scientists have uncovered a surprising genetic connection to spinal degeneration and found that an existing osteoporosis drug can prevent damaging mineral buildup in zebrafish spines. The discovery could pave the way for new treatments that slow or prevent a major cause of chronic back pain.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] NASA warns this year's Monster El Niño could be even bigger than legendary 1997 event
items.content_html: NASA scientists warn that the rapidly intensifying 2026 El Niño could surpass the historic 1997-98 event, which triggered devastating weather extremes around the world. Satellite data reveal striking similarities between the two, raising the possibility of major rainfall and flooding this winter, although the exact impacts remain uncertain.

items.content_html: Sometimes new species evade detection because they’re tiny and thus easy to miss—not this giant fungus. Shaped like a hand reaching out of the ground, this new species of fungus was discovered deep in the forest in China’s Yunnan Province. A research team from the Kunming Institute of Botany, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, reported it as a new species they named _Dianjunus rex_. items.title: [ScienceDaily] Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
items.content_html: Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered how to use flashes of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions inside a crystal, solving a decades-old mystery about how the material behaves. The laser-induced alignment lasts just a trillionth of a second, but the breakthrough could open the door to new ways of processing and storing information.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
items.content_html: Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.

items.title: [space.com] Apollo 12 lightning strikes prompted NASA to tighten launch weather rules
items.content_html: Lightning struck NASA’s Apollo 12 Saturn V rocket twice within seconds of its Nov. 14, 1969, launch, disrupting spacecraft telemetry and endangering the mission. Mission Control engineer John Aaron recognized the readings from an earlier test and recommended switching the Signal Conditioning Equipment to its auxiliary setting, which restored the data. Investigators concluded the rocket and its conductive exhaust plume had triggered a discharge in an electrically charged part of the atmosphere, even though no active thunderstorm lay along the immediate flight path. NASA expanded launch weather restrictions to account for atmospheric electrical conditions, not only visible lightning and thunderstorms.

items.title: [newspaceeconomy.ca] NASA identifies potential biosignature in Mars rock sample
items.content_html: Researchers are investigating Mars, Jupiter’s icy moons and other solar-system sites as possible habitats, but Earth remains the only world known to support life. NASA’s Perseverance rover collected a rock sample in July 2024 that the agency later described as containing a potential biosignature: organic material and mineral patterns that could reflect microbial activity but also have possible nonbiological explanations. Mars preserves evidence of ancient surface water, while Europa and Enceladus may hold oceans beneath ice. Habitable conditions do not establish that organisms exist; water, usable energy and accessible chemical ingredients must come together over time. NASA’s Europa Clipper and the European Space Agency’s JUICE mission are traveling to study Jupiter’s icy moons, where possible exchanges between surface and subsurface reservoirs also raise planetary-protection concerns.

items.title: [c-jcm.com] Cancer AI studies report support benefits, high accuracy and readability gaps
items.content_html: A study of 140 patients with pancreatic cancer found that those who used an AI assistant’s psychological-support feature had lower anxiety and quality-of-life scores than nonusers. More frequent overall use was also associated with lower anxiety, but the relationship was borderline statistically significant. Researchers assessed patients once in April and May 2026; the findings show an association, not that the tool caused the differences. Separate lung-cancer research found high accuracy in AI answers to patient questions, but all three systems tested produced text at a 10th- to 12th-grade reading level. Other cancer studies presented for a pathology meeting reported on AI applications for classifying tumors, drafting molecular reports and deciding when rapid testing could be deferred.

items.title: [scimex.org] Astronomers trace eight-minute radio pulses to white dwarf and Sun-like star
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers have traced repeating radio pulses from the system GPM J071507−114153 to a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like star—the first known long-period radio transient with this type of stellar pairing. The pulses recur every 7.9 minutes but appear only during a roughly six-hour window in each 32-hour orbit. The system lies more than 5,000 light-years away. Researchers discovered the system using Australia’s Murchison Widefield Array, pinpointed it with South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope and used the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii to identify the companion as a G-type star. Measurements of the orbit and the companion’s slight movement indicate that the pulsing object has about two-thirds the Sun’s mass, making it too light to be a neutron star. The study was published in Nature Astronomy on Nov. 12, 2026.

items.title: [dlr.de] Europe’s Hera probe reveals Didymos ridge as asteroid-defense survey begins
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has begun its close study of the Didymos asteroid pair. New images show boulders, craters and a sharply defined ridge around Didymos’ equator. Hera is inspecting the system after NASA deliberately struck its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, in 2022 to test asteroid deflection. The images, taken from about 56 kilometers away, show a side of Didymos that NASA’s DART spacecraft did not see before impact. Scientists say Didymos’ rapid spin may help explain the ridge and could send surface material toward its equator or into space. Hera will continue its survey with 25 instruments. Two CubeSats are due to investigate Dimorphos at closer range, including with radar and an attempted landing. The agency plans to release detailed images of both asteroids on Nov. 25.

items.title: [universetoday.com] Chandra links recurring stellar outbursts to hidden compact companion
items.content_html: Astronomers say AT 2016blu, in the galaxy NGC 4559 about 30 million light-years away, is not a supernova but a massive star whose repeated outbursts likely involve a black hole or neutron-star companion. The star has survived 27 recorded outbursts recurring roughly every 113 days since 2012. An observation by the Chandra X-ray Observatory timed to an outburst in March 2026 found the star was 100 times brighter in X-rays than in observations from 2001-02. Researchers say the companion draws in gas shed by the star during close orbital approaches, and the gas heats up and emits X-rays. They estimate that gas equivalent to about 2.7% of Earth’s mass transfers to the companion during each outburst.

items.title: [newscientist.com] Independent analysis confirms ring in M87* black hole image
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An independent reanalysis of Event Horizon Telescope observations has reproduced the bright ring surrounding the black hole's shadow in the first black hole image, confirming the central feature of the 2019 image of M87*. The study, published Nov. 11 in Nature, used a separate imaging method to address questions about whether image-processing choices had produced the ring. The team, led by CSIRO astronomers Samuel Lai and Nithyanandan Thyagarajan, analyzed observations from 2017, 2018 and 2021. The ring in the new images had an average diameter of 42.2 microarcseconds, consistent with an estimated black hole mass of 6.5 billion solar masses. The researchers said the result supports the ring-like shape predicted by general relativity, although fine details such as ring thickness and brightness distribution still vary with the method and data quality.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
items.content_html: A new study found that energy drinks and stimulant supplements were linked to disproportionately frequent reports of serious heart problems, including 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest and 4.5 times more reports of heart attacks. Young adults accounted for nearly half of the cardiovascular reports involving these products, raising concerns about their potential risks despite the study being unable to prove causation.

items.title: [zmescience.com] Mantle-driven uplift explains Earth's billion-year rock gap, study finds
items.content_html: A new model suggests slow circulation in Earth’s mantle lifted parts of three ancient continental regions, allowing ice sheets to erode rock layers and create the Great Unconformity, a gap in the geological record. The study by University of Wollongong researchers Santosh Dhungana and Nicolas Flament was published Nov. 4 in Nature. The model indicates Laurentia, Baltica and North China rose from roughly a billion years ago to about 540 million years ago, then began sinking, allowing younger sediments to accumulate. Flament said glaciation likely drove much of the erosion, but mantle uplift created the slopes glaciers needed to carry sediment away.
